instructions:
Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 291 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool scored the draft on how it carries feeling. For each measure below it gives the current value and a target. Revise the essay so that its measures move to the targets; the tool will score the result again.
- positive charge (hedons per 1,000 words): now 87.1, target 68.9. Counts positive words such as good, love, fun.
- negative charge (dolors per 1,000 words): now 10.0, target 23.9. Counts negative words such as bad, hate, problem.
- words that carry charge (% of words): now 26.5, target 24.3. Counts share of all words that carry any feeling.
- charge under a negation (% of charge): now 4.2, target 1.4. Counts feeling words placed under not, never or n't.
- charge after an intensifier such as 'very' (% of charge): now 1.1, target 0.0. Counts feeling words placed right after very, really or so.
- charge after a contrast word such as 'but' (% of charge): now 6.3, target 0.0. Counts feeling words placed after but or however in the same sentence.
- net charge of the last fifth minus the text's mean (per 1,000 words): now 28.0, target -3.0. Counts how much more positive the last fifth is than the essay as a whole; negative means a more downbeat ending.
- how unevenly charge is spread over sentences (1 = as if words were dealt at random): now 1.3, target 1.0. Counts above 1 means the feeling is bunched into some sentences while others are plain; below 1 means it is spread evenly.

Draft:

Dear Principal,

I am writing to ask you not to adopt the policy that would require a B average to take part in sports and other activities. I understand the goal of pushing students to work harder in class, but I believe this rule would hurt the very students it is meant to help.

First, many students at our school have a C average, and a C is still a passing grade. These students are doing the work and meeting the standard. Taking away the one thing that keeps some of them excited about school could make them care less about their classes, not more. For a lot of kids, practice after school is the reason they show up in the morning.

Second, sports and clubs teach lessons that do not show up on a report card. On the soccer team or in the drama club, students learn teamwork, responsibility, and how to handle losing. They learn to manage their time because they have to balance homework with practice. These skills matter for jobs and for life, and a student with a C needs them just as much as a student with an A.

Third, activities give students adults who care about them. Coaches and club advisors often notice when a student is struggling and push them to get help. If we remove those students from teams, we also remove that support.

Instead of a B requirement, I suggest keeping the C average rule and adding a tutoring program for players whose grades slip. That way, students stay involved while getting the help they need to improve.

Thank you for asking for our views. I hope you will keep activities open to every student who is passing.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student
